content.q: What is recursion? Show it with a picture.
content.title: Recursion
content.text:
Imagine a stack of boxes: each box asks you to open a smaller one until you reach an empty box. **Recursion** is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version.

[new word] recursion: A way to solve a problem by having a function call itself on a smaller version. (like Opening smaller boxes until one is empty.)

The picture follows the calls from `sum_to(4)` down to `sum_to(0)`, then back up; see [[10-11|the call and its picture]]. The returned total is `4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0`, so [[12|the printed result]] is `10`.

[quiz] What number does this code print? | choices: 0) 4 1) 10 2) 0 | answer: 1 | why: Each call adds its number after the smaller call returns: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 10.

[next questions] How can recursion draw a maze? / Where do apps use nested folders? / How do loops solve the same problem?

The code returns a (total, picture) tuple and builds dicts alongside the arithmetic. A beginner has to untangle that before seeing plain recursion, so the picture code hides the idea. Lines 8-9 have no plain-English note either.

content.q: How does binary search find a number so fast?
content.title: Find it fast
content.text:
Imagine looking for a name in an alphabetized guest list: check the middle, then ignore the half that cannot contain it. That’s **binary search**: finding a value by repeatedly cutting a sorted list in half.

[new word] binary search: A way to find a value in a sorted list by repeatedly checking the middle and discarding half. (like Finding a page by jumping halfway through a book.)

The list must already be sorted. Here, we look for `23`; [[7-9|these lines]] check the middle value, and [[12-15|these lines]] keep only the half where `23` could be.

The first middle value is `16`, which is smaller than `23`, so the left half is ruled out. Next comes `38`, then `23`; the search takes just three checks here. [[8|This line]] uses whole-number division to choose a middle position.

If the middle matches, `break` ends the search. Otherwise, the next pass shrinks the range; this is why binary search can be much faster than checking every item, especially in a long, sorted list.

[quiz] If the middle value is 16 and the target is 23, which side stays in the search? | choices: 0) The left side 1) The right side 2) Both sides | answer: 1 | why: The list is sorted, so values left of 16 are even smaller.

[try] Change target from 23 to 72 / Change target from 23 to 2 / Add 30 between 23 and 38

[next questions] How many checks for 100 numbers? / Where do apps use sorted lists? / How does binary search compare with linear search?
content.code:
numbers = [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72]
target = 23
low = 0
high = len(numbers) - 1
checks = []

while low <= high:
    middle = (low + high) // 2
    checks.append(numbers[middle])
    if numbers[middle] == target:
        break
    if numbers[middle] < target:
        low = middle + 1
    else:
        high = middle - 1

show(numbers, "Sorted numbers")
show({"target": target, "checked": checks}, "What got checked")

content.q: What is a variable? I have never written code before.

[new word] variable: A name that lets your code remember and reuse a value. (like A label on a lunchbox.)

The second picture shows “cookie” and `8`: changing a name's value changes what the name gives back. [[6-7|watch both changes]] Then [[9|look at the result]]—the names still work, but their values are different.

content.q: How does consistent hashing spread keys across servers, and what moves when a server is added?
content.title: Consistent hashing
content.text:
Imagine a circular neighborhood: each key walks clockwise until it meets a server. **Consistent hashing** places keys and servers on the same circle, so each key has a predictable owner.

[new word] consistent hashing: A way to place keys and servers on a circle so adding a server changes only some assignments. (like A circular neighborhood where only nearby homes change.)

A **hash function** turns a name into the same number every time; sorting those numbers makes the circle. This example gives each server three points to smooth out uneven gaps.

[new word] hash function: A rule that turns a name into the same number every time. (like A name always gets the same seat number.)

The lookup follows the sorted circle [[14-17|to find a key's owner]]. After D joins, the comparison [[21-25|shows which keys moved]]. Only keys whose clockwise path now reaches D first change owners; the rest stay put.

Three points per server help reduce uneven gaps, but they cannot guarantee perfect balance. More points can smooth distribution further, at the cost of a larger ring; this small example keeps the trade-off easy to see [[7-12|in the ring builder]].

[quiz] A key belonged to B before D joined. What can happen? | choices: 0) It moves to D if D appears first clockwise. 1) It must move to D. 2) It moves to another old server because D joined. | answer: 0 | why: Existing points stay put; only keys whose clockwise route reaches D first change owners.

content.q: What is recursion? Show it with a picture.
content.title: Recursion
content.text:
Picture a set of Russian nesting dolls. To find the smallest doll, you open one and ask the same question of the doll inside, until you reach one that opens no further.

**Recursion** is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of it. The code below calls `fib` on smaller numbers, and records every call as a tree you can see.

[new word] recursion: A function that solves a big problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the problem. (like Opening nesting dolls until you hit the tiny one.)

Every recursive function needs two parts. The [[2-3|base case]] is the tiny problem it can answer directly. The [[4-5|recursive calls]] shrink the problem and trust the function to solve the smaller piece.

[new word] base case: The simplest version of the problem, answered directly without any more self-calls. (like The smallest doll that doesn't open.)

Look at the tree when you run it. The top is `fib(4)`, and each branch is a smaller call. Leaves are base cases. Then [[6|the addition]] runs from the bottom up: 1+0 gives fib(2)=1, and so on up to 3 at the root.

[quiz] What happens if you delete the base case (lines 2–3)? | choices: 0) It returns 0 for everything 1) fib keeps calling itself and crashes with RecursionError 2) It runs once and stops | answer: 1 | why: Nothing stops the calls from shrinking past 0 into negative numbers, so Python eventually gives up with a RecursionError.

content.q: How does binary search find a number so fast?
content.title: Binary search
content.text:
Imagine guessing a number from 1 to 100 where I only say "higher" or "lower". You'd guess 50, not 1. Every answer lets you **throw away half** of what's left.

That's binary search. It only works on a **sorted** list, and it needs about 7 checks for 100 items instead of up to 100. The code below logs every guess so you can watch the zone shrink.

The list has 33 items. [[4|The loop]] runs while the zone still has room. Each time, [[5|we look at the middle]]. Sorted order is the trick: if the middle is too small, everything left of it is too small as well.

[new word] sorted: Arranged in order, here smallest to largest, so position tells you something about size. (like Like words in a dictionary.)

So [[10-13|we discard a whole half]] by moving `lo` or `hi`. Searching for 72 takes 5 guesses: 51, 75, 63, 69, then 72. A one-by-one scan would need 24. Doubling the list adds just **one** more guess, which is called **logarithmic** growth.

[new word] logarithmic: Growth where doubling the input adds only one extra step. (like Like folding a paper in half again and again.)

[quiz] The first guess is 51, which is less than 72. What happens next? | choices: 0) lo becomes 17, skipping everything up to 51 1) hi becomes 15, searching the left side 2) mid becomes 0 and we restart | answer: 0 | why: 51 is at index 16 and is too small, so line 11 sets lo = 16 + 1 = 17. Everything left of it is smaller still.

[try] Change 72 to 5 / Change 100 to 3000 / Change 72 to 3

[next questions] Why must the list be sorted? / Where do apps use binary search? / What is Big-O notation?
content.code:
def binary_search(items, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(items) - 1
    steps = []
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        steps.append({"lo": lo, "mid": mid, "hi": hi, "value": items[mid]})
        if items[mid] == target:
            show(steps, "found it")
            return mid
        if items[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    show(steps, "not found")
    return -1

numbers = list(range(3, 100, 3))
show(numbers, "sorted list")
print(binary_search(numbers, 72))

2-2: the zone: lo and hi are the edges of where the target could still be. At first, everywhere.

content.q: How does consistent hashing spread keys across servers, and what moves when a server is added?
content.title: Consistent hashing
content.text:
Picture a clock face. Each server is pinned at many spots on the rim, and each key lands on the rim too. A key belongs to the first server pin you meet walking clockwise.

The naive way, `hash(key) % N`, reshuffles almost everything when N changes. On a ring, adding a server only claims the arcs just before its new pins. Everything else stays put.

Each server gets 50 **virtual nodes**, scattered pins on the ring ([[7|line 7]]). Looking up a key hashes it and takes the [[10|first pin clockwise]]. That is one binary search over the sorted pins, so O(log(servers × vnodes)).

[new word] virtual node: One of many ring positions that all point to the same physical server. (like One shop owning many market stalls spread around a square.)

Adding D inserts new pins and nothing else. A key either keeps its old owner or moves to D, never between A, B and C. Expect about 1/4 of keys to move, versus about 3/4 in [[19-20|the mod-N comparison]].

Trade-offs: more vnodes give better balance but a bigger ring and more memory. Moved keys still need a data migration, and replication usually walks on to the next distinct servers. Real systems like Dynamo-style stores and CDNs add those layers.

[quiz] After adding server D, where can a key that changed owner have gone? | choices: 0) Only to D 1) To any of A, B, C or D 2) Only to the server after D | answer: 0 | why: D only adds pins. A key's nearest clockwise pin either stays the same or becomes one of D's new pins, so keys never shuffle among A, B and C.

[try] Change vnodes=50 to 1 / Change "ABCD" to "ABCDE" in new_ring / Change 2**32 to 360

[next questions] Why do vnodes balance load better? / Where do CDNs and caches use this? / How does replication work on a ring?
content.code:
import bisect, hashlib

def h(s):
    return int(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 2**32

def build_ring(servers, vnodes=50):
    return sorted((h(f"{s}#{i}"), s) for s in servers for i in range(vnodes))

def lookup(ring, key):
    i = bisect.bisect(ring, (h(key), "")) % len(ring)
    return ring[i][1]

keys = [f"user{i}" for i in range(1000)]
old_ring = build_ring("ABC")
new_ring = build_ring("ABCD")
old = [lookup(old_ring, k) for k in keys]
new = [lookup(new_ring, k) for k in keys]

moved = sum(a != b for a, b in zip(old, new))
naive = sum(h(k) % 3 != h(k) % 4 for k in keys)
rows = [{"server": s, "before": old.count(s), "after": new.count(s)} for s in "ABCD"]
show(rows, "keys per server")
show({"ring moved": moved, "mod-N moved": naive, "keys": len(keys)}, "keys that changed server")

content.q: How do promises and async/await work in JavaScript?
content.title: Promises and async/await
content.text:
Picture ordering at a café. You get a buzzer, not your food. You can scroll your phone while the kitchen works, and the buzzer goes off when your order is ready (or if they ran out of bread).

A **promise** is that buzzer: an object standing in for a value that isn't ready yet. `async/await` is a calmer way to write code that waits for those buzzers.

[new word] promise: An object that represents a result that will arrive later, either a value or an error. (like A restaurant buzzer for your order.)

Look at [[6|the promise]]: it starts pending, and when the timer fires it calls `resolve`, which settles it with a value. Anyone holding it can attach `.then(...)` (as on [[19|the juice]]) to run code when it arrives.

[[11|The await]] is the same idea with nicer syntax. The function pauses there and resumes with the value, as if it were a normal variable. That's why [[17-18|these two lines]] run straight away: `makeToast()` starts, hits its first `await`, and hands back a promise. Then [[20|Promise.all]] waits for both to finish.

Run it and read the table: the toast starts and the order is placed at about 0ms, the juice arrives near 100ms, and the bread near 200ms. The two waits overlapped instead of adding up to 300ms. For errors, a rejected promise throws at `await`, so you can wrap it in `try/catch`.

[new word] async function: A function that always returns a promise and may pause at await without freezing the rest of the program. (like A cook who walks away while the oven works.)

[quiz] After "order placed" is logged, what is logged next? | choices: 0) toast: start 1) got bread 2) not waiting, doing other work | answer: 0 | why: An async function runs normally until its first await. content.q: What is recursion? Show it with a picture.
content.title: Recursion: a function that calls itself
content.text:
Picture a stack of Russian nesting dolls. To find the smallest doll, you open one and get *the same problem, just smaller*. You keep opening until there's a doll that doesn't open. That's the whole trick.

In code, **recursion** means a function solves a problem by calling *itself* on a smaller version of it. Below, `fib` also records every call it makes, so you can **see** the calls branch out as a tree.

[new word] recursion: When a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of the same problem. (like Opening nesting dolls until one won't open.)

Every recursive function needs two parts. The **base case** at [[3-4|lines 3–4]] is a problem so small you just *know* the answer: `fib(0)` is 0 and `fib(1)` is 1. No more calls are made there. These are the leaves at the bottom of the picture.

[new word] base case: The smallest version of the problem, answered directly so the self-calls finally stop. (like The tiny solid doll in the middle.)

The **recursive step** at [[6-7|lines 6–7]] trusts that `fib` already works for smaller numbers. So `fib(4)` asks `fib(3)` and `fib(2)`, and each of those asks again. That's why one call becomes a branching tree: **9 calls** in total to get the answer 3.

Answers flow *back up*. The leaves return first, then [[8|line 8]] adds the two results, and each parent finishes only after its children do. [[14|This line]] draws the tree of calls, and the final value is printed on line 15. Notice `fib(2)` appears twice: plain recursion often repeats work.

[quiz] What happens if you delete lines 3–4 (the base case)? | choices: 0) fib(4) still returns 3 1) It stops at fib(0) automatically 2) It calls itself forever until Python raises RecursionError | answer: 2 | why: Without a base case nothing stops the calls: fib(0) calls fib(-1), then fib(-2), and so on, until Python gives up with a RecursionError.

content.q: How does binary search find a number so fast?
content.title: Binary search: halving your way to the answer
content.text:
Think of guessing a number between 1 and 100 when someone says "higher" or "lower". You don't start at 1. You guess 50, and one answer wipes out **half** the possibilities. Then you guess the middle of what's left, and so on.

**Binary search** does exactly this on a **sorted** list. Each check throws away half the list, so even huge lists need only a handful of looks.

[new word] binary search: A way to find a value in a sorted list by checking the middle and discarding the half it can't be in. (like Opening a dictionary near the middle, then flipping toward your word.)

Every pass through [[4-13|the loop]] looks at [[5|the middle]] of the range `lo`..`hi`. If that value is too small, the target must be to the right, so [[10-11|lo jumps past mid]]. Too big? [[12-13|hi jumps below mid]]. Either way, half the remaining list vanishes.

Run it and watch the table: searching for 9 in 33 numbers takes 5 guesses. The range shrinks 33 → 16 → 7 → 3 → 1. A plain left-to-right scan would need 3 checks here, but for 99 it would need 33. Binary search never needs more than 6 for this list.

That's the secret to its speed: the number of steps grows with how many times you can **halve** n, not with n itself. A million items need about 20 guesses. A billion need about 30. We call this **O(log n)** time.

[new word] O(log n): The work grows by one step each time the input size doubles. (like Doubling a phone book adds just one more flip.)

[quiz] If the list grew from 33 numbers to 66, how many extra guesses would binary search need at most? | choices: 0) About 1 more 1) About twice as many 2) About 33 more | answer: 0 | why: One extra guess cuts 66 down to 33, and from there it's the same search as before. Doubling the list adds just one step.

[next questions] What if the list has duplicate numbers? / Where do apps use binary search? / How do binary search trees work?

def binary_search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    steps = []
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        steps.append({"lo": lo, "mid": mid, "hi": hi, "value": nums[mid]})
        if nums[mid] == target:
            show(steps, "each guess")
            return mid
        elif nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    show(steps, "each guess")
    return -1

nums = list(range(3, 100, 3))
show(nums, "sorted list")
index = binary_search(nums, 9)
print("found 9 at index", index)

content.q: Make a tiny web page with a button that counts clicks.
content.title: A click-counting button
content.text:
A click counter is like a tally clicker a bouncer holds at the door. Each press adds one, and the little window shows the new total. Our page does the same with three parts: a number to show, a button to press, and a bit of JavaScript that connects them.

The JavaScript keeps the real count in [[18|this variable]]. Each click adds one to it and copies the new value into [[13|the number on screen]].

content.q: How does consistent hashing spread keys across servers, and what moves when a server is added?
content.title: Consistent hashing: a ring of servers
content.text:
Say you split 1000 cache keys across 3 servers with `hash(key) % 3`. Then you add a 4th server and switch to `% 4`. That changes almost every key's server, so about 75% of your cache is suddenly in the wrong place. **Consistent hashing** fixes this by making a new server take over only a small slice of the keys.

[new word] consistent hashing: A way to map keys to servers where adding or removing a server moves only about 1/N of the keys. (like Adding one more seat at a round table, not reshuffling everyone.)

The picture to keep in mind is a clock face. Servers and keys are hashed onto the same circle of 2³² positions. A key belongs to the first server point you reach going clockwise from it. Each server gets 100 points on the ring, not one, so the circle is cut into fair-sized arcs.

[new word] virtual nodes: Many hashed positions per physical server on the ring, which evens out how many keys each server gets. (like Buying 100 raffle tickets instead of one to get a fair share.)

[[8-10|build_ring]] hashes `A#0`…`A#99` and the same for every other server, then sorts all the points. Looking up a key in [[13|this line]] is a binary search over those 300 or 400 points, so it costs O(log(N·v)). The `% len(points)` is what closes the line into a ring.

Here is what to expect when you run it. The table shows A, B and C each dropping from about 333 keys to about 236, while D picks up about 291. The [[24-25|moves table]] only has rows of the form `X -> D`. When D joins, it takes over the parts of the arcs just before its points, so no key moves between two old servers.

[[26|The naive line]] is the comparison. `h % 3` and `h % 4` agree only when `h mod 12` is 0, 1 or 2, so about 75% of keys move. On the ring, about 29% move (291 of 1000 in this run), which is close to the ideal 1/(N+1), or 25%. There are trade-offs. More vnodes give a more even split but use more memory, take longer to rebuild, and add a few binary-search steps. Real systems also give servers different weights by changing how many vnodes each one gets.

[quiz] After adding D, which rows can appear in the 'where moved keys went' table? | choices: 0) Only rows like A -> D, B -> D, C -> D 1) Any pair, like A -> B, because the whole ring is rebuilt 2) Only D -> A style rows, because D gives keys away | answer: 0 | why: Adding D's points only splits existing arcs. Each key's next point clockwise is either the same as before or one of D's new points.

[next questions] How do weighted servers get more vnodes? / Where do DynamoDB and Cassandra use rings? / What is rendezvous (HRW) hashing instead?
content.code:
import hashlib
from bisect import bisect
from collections import Counter

def h(s):
    return int(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 2**32

def build_ring(servers, vnodes=100):
    ring = sorted((h(f"{s}#{i}"), s) for s in servers for i in range(vnodes))
    return [p for p, _ in ring], [s for _, s in ring]

def owner(key, points, names):
    i = bisect(points, h(key)) % len(points)
    return names[i]

keys = [f"user:{n}" for n in range(1000)]
ring3, ring4 = build_ring("ABC"), build_ring("ABCD")
old = {k: owner(k, *ring3) for k in keys}
new = {k: owner(k, *ring4) for k in keys}

c_old, c_new = Counter(old.values()), Counter(new.values())
show([{"server": s, "before": c_old[s], "after": c_new[s]} for s in "ABCD"],
     "keys per server")
moves = Counter(f"{old[k]} -> {new[k]}" for k in keys if old[k] != new[k])
show(dict(moves), "where moved keys went")
naive = sum(h(k) % 3 != h(k) % 4 for k in keys)
print(f"ring moved {sum(moves.values())} keys; hash % N would move {naive}")

content.q: How do promises and async/await work in JavaScript?
content.title: Promises and async/await
content.text:
Picture ordering at a café. You get a **buzzer** right away, then you go find a seat instead of standing frozen at the counter. When your food is ready, the buzzer goes off and you go collect it.

JavaScript works the same way with slow jobs like timers and network calls. Below, we cook a pretend breakfast and record **when** each thing really happens.

[new word] promise: An object that stands for a value that isn't ready yet but will arrive later, or fail. (like A café buzzer: proof your order is coming.)

[[5-9|wait]] builds a promise by hand: it returns the buzzer instantly, and `setTimeout` calls `resolve` later. Until then the promise is **pending**; after `resolve` it's **fulfilled** and carries a value.

[new word] async/await: Keywords that let you write promise code top to bottom: `await` pauses a function until a promise finishes. (like Reading a recipe step by step, waiting where it says 'bake'.)

Look at the timeline it shows. An async function runs normally **until its first await**, so "start toast" appears at 0 ms. Then [[13|the await]] pauses `makeBreakfast`, and control jumps back out to [[22|this line]]. That's why "keep going" is also at 0 ms, before any food arrives.

Toast lands near 300 ms. [[15|Promise.all]] starts eggs and tea together, so the pair is ready near 500 ms (300 + 200), not 600, while tea itself arrives near 400 ms. Finally [[24-27|then]] receives what `return` produced. `await` and `.then` are two ways to say the same thing.

[new word] event loop: The part of JavaScript that runs waiting callbacks, like finished timers, once the current code is done. (like A waiter checking which buzzers have gone off.)

content.q: What is recursion? Show it with a picture.
content.title: What is recursion?
content.text:
Imagine opening a nest of **Russian dolls**. Inside each doll is a smaller doll, until you reach one that cannot be opened. **Recursion** works the same way: a function solves a big problem by calling *itself* on a smaller piece, until the piece is so small the answer is obvious.

[new word] recursion: A way of solving a problem where a function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. (like Nested Russian dolls, each holding a smaller doll inside.)

Look at `countdown`: it prints 3, 2, 1 and then liftoff. Each call handles **one** step and hands the rest to a smaller copy of itself. The line [[5|print the number]] does the visible work, and [[6|the self-call]] passes the baton down.

`total` is the sneakier one. To add 1 through 4, it computes `4 + total(3)`, but it can't finish until `total(3)` returns. Each waiting call is stacked up like dolls, and the answers flow back out when the smallest one returns zero. [[11|Adding this number]] is where the answers get combined on the way back up.

## The picture of the calls

Here is every call to `total(4)`, drawn as a tree. Each node is one call, and it waits for its child.

[quiz] What happens if `total` had no base case (no `if n == 0` check)? | choices: 0) It returns 0 and stops 1) It keeps calling itself until Python runs out of memory and crashes 2) It adds the numbers in reverse order | answer: 1 | why: Without a stopping point, every call creates another call. Python caps the depth and raises a RecursionError rather than running forever.

content.q: How does binary search find a number so fast?
content.title: Binary search: finding things by halving
content.text:
Imagine guessing a number from 1 to 100. If you guess 50 and I say **higher**, you just threw away half the choices in one move. Binary search does exactly that, again and again, on a **sorted** list.

Each time you check the **middle** of the current range, you cut the remaining possibilities in half. With 64 numbers you need up to 7 checks, because 64 halves to 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, and one more check is needed to finish. Look at the step records: the range shrinks fast. That shrinking is the whole trick.

[new word] sorted list: A list where every item is in order, smallest to largest, or the reverse. (like A phone book, where names are in alphabetical order.)

The math behind the speed is called **logarithmic time**. For n items, binary search needs about log2(n) checks. A million items takes only about 20 checks, while a plain scan could need a million. This is why it is one of the most important tools in programming.

[quiz] Why does binary search need the list to be sorted? | choices: 0) So it knows which half to throw away after each check 1) So the list uses less memory 2) So the middle element is always the target | answer: 0 | why: Sorting lets one comparison tell you which side the target must be on. Without order, a single check tells you nothing about the other half.

def binary_search(items, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(items) - 1
    steps = []
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        steps.append({"lo": lo, "mid": mid, "hi": hi, "value": items[mid]})
        if items[mid] == target:
            show(steps, "search steps")
            return mid
        elif items[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    show(steps, "search steps")
    return -1

numbers = list(range(0, 64, 2))
print("index of 22:", binary_search(numbers, 22))
print("index of 23:", binary_search(numbers, 23))

content.q: How does consistent hashing spread keys across servers, and what moves when a server is added?

[new word] consistent hashing: A way to assign keys to servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of keys. (like Seats at a round table: each guest sits with the nearest chair to their left.)

content.q: How do promises and async/await work in JavaScript?
content.title: Promises and async/await
content.text:
Some work takes time: fetching data, waiting for a timer, reading a file. JavaScript doesn't freeze while waiting. It keeps running and comes back when the result is ready.

Think of a **promise** as a receipt from a coffee shop. You don't have the coffee yet, but you hold a ticket that will become the drink. Later, the barista calls your name, or tells you the order failed.

[new word] promise: An object representing a value that will be available later, or an error. (like A receipt for an order that isn't ready yet.)

Here is the order. `main()` starts, prints **start**, and hits the first `await` on [[14|the coffee line]]. It pauses on [[15|the coffee line]], so the function returns early. The last line prints **main() returned early** straight away.

After 500 ms, the promise resolves with `'latte'`, and `main()` resumes on [[16|the log line]]. Each `await` is a pause point. The **async** keyword just says that a function can contain them and always returns a promise itself.

[new word] async function: A function that can pause at await and always returns a promise. (like A recipe that can say 'wait here until the oven beeps.')

[quiz] What prints first when this code runs? | choices: 0) start 1) main() returned early 2) got latte | answer: 0 | why: main() runs synchronously until its first await. Then the code after main() runs before any timer fires, so 'start' comes first, then 'main() returned early', and 'got latte' only after 500 ms.

content.q: What is recursion? Show it with a picture.
content.title: Thinking in loops that call themselves
content.text:
Imagine Russian nesting dolls: to open the whole set, you open one doll, peek inside, and find another doll waiting. You repeat the exact same ritual until you hit the tiniest solid wooden doll.

In code, **recursion** happens when a function solves a big puzzle by calling itself on a slightly smaller piece, stopping only when it hits a **base case**.

[new word] recursion: A technique where a function solves a problem by calling a smaller version of itself. (like Looking between two parallel mirrors and seeing endless reflections.)

Look at [[2-3|the first two lines]]: whenever `n` dwindles to zero, the function returns immediately without spawning more calls. That is our stop sign.

When `n` is greater than zero, [[4-5|lines 4 and 5]] ask `countdown` to solve `n - 1`. Because each call branches twice, [[8|countdown(3)]] unfolds into a branching tree of smaller tasks before folding back up into a single nested dictionary.

content.q: How does binary search find a number so fast?
content.title: Binary search
content.text:
Imagine guessing a secret number between 1 and 100. If you guess 50 and hear "higher", you just eliminated 50 numbers in a single move.

That strategy is called **binary search**. Because the list is sorted, checking [[5|the middle element]] splits the remaining choices in half every single step.

[new word] binary search: An algorithm that finds an item in a sorted list by repeatedly checking the middle element. (like Opening a dictionary right in the middle to find a word.)

Notice how [[6|steps]] tracks each guess. Looking for 68 among 9 numbers takes only 2 checks because each comparison discards an entire half.

If we double the list to 1,000 items, binary search needs only about 10 steps. That logarithmic growth makes it virtually instant even on billions of items.

[quiz] Why must the input list be sorted before running binary search? | choices: 0) Without order, checking the middle tells you nothing about where the target lives 1) Unsorted lists cause integer division to fail 2) Python's while loop only works on sorted lists | answer: 0 | why: Binary search relies on knowing whether the target lies to the left or right of the middle; without sorted order, you cannot rule out any half.

[try] Change 68 to 91 / Change 68 to 100 / Change nums[mid] < target to >

[next questions] What if the list has duplicates? / How do database indexes use this? / What is logarithmic time complexity?

def binary_search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    steps = []
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        steps.append({"lo": lo, "mid": mid, "hi": hi, "val": nums[mid]})
        if nums[mid] == target:
            show(steps, "Search steps")
            return mid
        elif nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    show(steps, "Search steps")
    return -1

content.q: How does consistent hashing spread keys across servers, and what moves when a server is added?
content.title: Consistent hashing & server churn
content.text:
Standard `hash(key) % N` remaps nearly every key when server count $N$ changes. **Consistent hashing** arranges both servers and keys onto a shared continuous circle (ring), mapping each key to the next clockwise server.

[new word] consistent hashing: A ring-based partitioning strategy where adding or removing a node only relocates $K/N$ keys on average. (like Passengers boarding whichever clockwise bus stop comes next on a loop.)

Notice how [[6-8|assigning keys]] searches for the nearest clockwise server on [[3|the ring]], meaning adding Server C only claims keys from its immediate clockwise neighbor instead of triggering a global shuffle.

In [[19-21|the comparison loop]], only keys falling into Node C's new ring segment transfer over from Node C's successor. The remaining partitions remain completely untouched, keeping cache churn strictly bounded.

In production systems, physical nodes use hundreds of **virtual nodes** (vnodes) across the ring to prevent hot spots and guarantee an even statistical key distribution.

[new word] virtual nodes: Multiple pseudo-positions assigned to one physical machine on the hash ring to balance load. (like One person laying down multiple towels to claim spread-out spots on a beach.)

[quiz] When adding an N-th server to a consistent hash ring of N-1 servers, what fraction of keys move? | choices: 0) Roughly 1 / N of all keys 1) Exactly (N - 1) / N of all keys 2) All keys except one 3) Zero keys until a rebalance runs | answer: 0 | why: Only the keys falling into the new node's ring segment relocate from its neighbor, averaging 1/N of total keys.

[try] Change range(12) to range(40) / Change srv_C to srv_Z / Swap bisect_right with bisect_left

import bisect, hashlib

def hash_val(val):
    return int(hashlib.md5(val.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 100

def get_node(ring, nodes, key):
    pos = bisect.bisect_right(ring, hash_val(key))
    return nodes[pos % len(nodes)]

keys = [f"key_{i}" for i in range(12)]
ring_ab = sorted([hash_val("srv_A"), hash_val("srv_B")])
nodes_ab = ["srv_A" if hash_val("srv_A") == r else "srv_B" for r in ring_ab]

ring_abc = sorted(ring_ab + [hash_val("srv_C")])
nodes_abc = [n for r in ring_abc for n in ["srv_A", "srv_B", "srv_C"] if hash_val(n) == r]

migrated = []
for k in keys:
    old_srv = get_node(ring_ab, nodes_ab, k)
    new_srv = get_node(ring_abc, nodes_abc, k)
    migrated.append({"key": k, "before": old_srv, "after": new_srv, "moved": old_srv != new_srv})

show(migrated)

content.q: What is recursion? Show it with a picture.
content.title: Seeing recursion as a tree
content.text:
Imagine holding two mirrors facing each other: you see infinite reflections of the same room, each nestled inside the next. In code, **recursion** happens when a function solves a problem by calling itself to handle a smaller piece.

[new word] recursion: A problem-solving technique where a function calls itself on a smaller input. (like Russian nesting dolls opening one inside another.)

Without an exit door, the function runs forever. That exit is the **base case**: [[2-3|the stopping check]] that returns an immediate answer without making any more calls.

[new word] base case: The condition that stops a recursive function from calling itself again. (like The tiny solid doll at the center.)

When you run [[8|calls = fib(3)]], Python does not compute the answer in one leap. It splits into two smaller calls: `fib(2)` and `fib(1)`. Then `fib(2)` splits again into `fib(1)` and `fib(0)`.

Look at [[4-5|the two recursive calls]]. Because each step branches into two until hitting [[2-3|the base case]], the history of calls forms a branching tree. The branches build up a tree structure of calls, which show() then draws.

[quiz] What happens if you delete lines 2 and 3? | choices: 0) Python crashes with a recursion error 1) The function returns 0 immediately 2) It calculates only the left branch | answer: 0 | why: Without a base case, the function calls itself with smaller negative numbers forever until Python hits its recursion depth limit.

content.q: How does binary search find a number so fast?
content.title: Binary search
content.text:
Imagine guessing a secret number between 1 and 100. If you guess 50 and hear "too low", you immediately rule out 50 possibilities in one breath. That divide-and-conquer strategy is called **binary search**.

[new word] binary search: An algorithm that repeatedly halves a sorted list to find a target value quickly. (like Opening a phone book right in the middle to find a name.)

In [[4|the while loop]], the algorithm tracks two boundary pointers: `lo` and `hi`. Each turn calculates [[5|the midpoint index]]. By checking just that single middle value on [[7|line 7]], we instantly know whether our target hides in the left or right half.

When our guess is too small on [[9-10|lines 9–10]], we push `lo` past the midpoint. Every single comparison cuts the remaining candidates in half. With 12 numbers, it takes at most 4 checks; with a million numbers, it takes just 20 checks!

[quiz] Why must the list be sorted before binary search can work? | choices: 0) So the computer can calculate the middle index using math 1) Because halving relies on knowing which side smaller or larger items live on 2) Because unsorted lists cause an error when comparing values | answer: 1 | why: If the list were jumbled, knowing that your target is larger than the middle number wouldn't tell you which half to discard.

[try] Change 56 to 3 / Change 56 to 100 to miss / Swap data with [10, 2, 8]

[next questions] What happens when target is not there? / How does git bisect find bugs? / What is a binary search tree?

def binary_search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    steps = []
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        steps.append({"step": len(steps) + 1, "lo": lo, "mid": mid, "hi": hi, "guess": nums[mid]})
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid, steps
        elif nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1, steps

idx, trace = binary_search(data, 56)
show(trace)
print(f"Found 56 at index {idx} in {len(trace)} steps!")

[new word] consistent hashing: A routing scheme where changing server count moves only a small fraction of keys. (like Musical chairs where adding a chair only shifts the nearest person.)

Keys travel clockwise along [[3|the ring]] to the first node they find. When we add node `40` at [[11|line 11]], only keys sitting on the arc between `15` and `40` must move.

content.q: How does binary search find a number so fast?
content.title: Binary search
content.text:
Imagine guessing a secret number between 1 and 100. If you guess 50 and hear "too low", you instantly rule out 50 numbers in a single breath. That is **binary search**: cutting your search space in half with every single check.

[new word] binary search: An algorithm that finds an item in a sorted list by repeatedly checking the middle element and halving the search area. (like Opening a phone book right down the middle to find a name.)

Because [[16|our list]] is already sorted, checking the middle element at [[5|line 5]] tells us for sure whether our target sits to the left or right.

Look at how rapidly the search window shrinks in [[4-12|the loop]]. Starting with 10 elements, we check index 4, eliminate the entire left side, and hit 23 on step three. Instead of crawling item by item, we discard half the possibilities each time.

This efficiency is known as **logarithmic time**. Even with one million items, binary search needs at most 20 comparisons to pinpoint any item or prove it missing.

[new word] logarithmic time: Performance where each additional step doubles the amount of data the algorithm can handle, written as O(log n). (like Finding one word among a million in just 20 page flips.)

[quiz] Why does binary search require the input list to be sorted? | choices: 0) To guarantee that discarding half never loses the target 1) Because Python can only calculate the middle of sorted lists 2) To prevent duplicate numbers from appearing in the list | answer: 0 | why: If the list were unsorted, a smaller number could hide on the right side and get thrown away by mistake!

def binary_search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    steps = []
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        steps.append({"lo": lo, "mid": mid, "hi": hi, "val": nums[mid]})
        if nums[mid] == target:
            break
        elif nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    show(steps, "Search steps")
    return mid if lo <= hi else -1

content.q: How does consistent hashing spread keys across servers, and what moves when a server is added?
content.title: Consistent hashing and server joins
content.text:
With naive modulo hashing (`hash(key) % N`), adding a server changes the divisor, remapping almost every key to a different machine and wrecking cache hit rates. **Consistent hashing** decouples key assignment from cluster size by mapping keys and servers onto the same mathematical ring.

[new word] consistent hashing: A partitioning scheme where adding or removing a node moves only a small fraction of keys across the cluster. (like Adding a toll booth that only takes cars from the lane right next to it.)

Both keys and servers hash to positions on a circular **hash ring**. A key routes clockwise to the first server it encounters. When a new server joins, it claims only the slice between itself and its counter-clockwise predecessor.

[new word] hash ring: A circular space where keys and servers map to angle coordinates and route clockwise to the nearest server. (like A circular track where each runner grabs relay batons dropped immediately behind them.)

On [[9|line 9]], `bisect_left` finds the target server in $O(\log S)$ time by scanning the sorted coordinates. When a key hashes past the final server's angle, the modulo operator wraps the index back to `0`, completing the ring without special-case branching.

When [[13|node-D joins]], only keys in its assigned arc shift from their previous owner. As shown in [[15-18|the table summary]], instead of reshuffling all items like naive hashing does, consistent hashing migrates only roughly $1/(N+1)$ of the keys (here, 1 in 4).

In production systems like Dynamo or Cassandra, raw node points cause uneven hash buckets and hot spots. Systems fix this by creating multiple **virtual nodes** per physical machine, spreading load uniformly across the token ring.

[new word] virtual nodes: Multiple pseudo-positions assigned to one physical machine on the ring to distribute partitions uniformly. (like Giving one clerk several ticket windows around an arena to balance customer lines.)

[quiz] In a cluster of 9 servers using consistent hashing, what fraction of keys migrate when a 10th server is added? | choices: 0) Roughly 10% (1/10) 1) Roughly 50% (1/2) 2) Roughly 90% (9/10) 3) 100% of all keys | answer: 0 | why: Only the keys falling into the arc claimed by the new server move from its neighbor; across N servers that averages 1/(N+1).

def h(key):
    return int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 360

def route(keys, nodes):
    ring = sorted((h(n), n) for n in nodes)
    pts = [pos for pos, _ in ring]
    return {k: ring[bisect.bisect_left(pts, h(k)) % len(ring)][1] for k in keys}

content.q: How do promises and async/await work in JavaScript?
content.title: Promises and async/await
content.text:
JavaScript runs on a single track. When a task takes time, like downloading a file, freezing the page would ruin the experience. Instead, a **promise** hands you a receipt for future work while the engine keeps running.

[new word] promise: An object representing a value that is not ready yet but will finish later. (like A buzzer at a cafe that beeps when your meal is ready.)

With **async/await**, you can pause inside a function until that receipt is fulfilled without stalling the rest of your program, as seen when [[16-17|calling makeBreakfast]].

[new word] async/await: Keywords that let asynchronous code pause and resume while reading like plain sequential steps. (like Putting a bookmark in a book while you answer the doorbell.)

Notice the timeline order. Even though [[16|makeBreakfast]] was invoked before [[17|pouring juice]], juice gets poured at `0ms`! When JavaScript hits [[8|await delay(60)]], it suspends `makeBreakfast` and jumps straight to the next line outside.

After 60 milliseconds elapse, the timer promise resolves. The JavaScript event loop wakes `makeBreakfast` back up to record the popped toast, then pauses again at [[10|line 10]]. You get clean, sequential code without freezing your app.

The main script continues immediately to pour juice.

content.q: What is recursion? Show it with a picture.
content.title: Recursion
content.text:
Imagine you're stacking Russian dolls. To open the biggest one you open a slightly smaller one, then a smaller one, then one so tiny it has nothing inside — that's your stopping point. **Recursion** is when a function calls itself, breaking a big problem into the same smaller shape, until it hits a base case small enough to answer directly.

[new word] base case: The simplest input a recursive function can answer without calling itself again. (like The smallest doll — solid inside, nothing more to open.)

The classic example is the **factorial**: `5!` = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1. Notice that `5!` = 5 × `4!`. That self-similar pattern is the heart of [[8-11|the recursive step]]. The chain stops at [[4-6|the base case]] — `0! = 1` — which every branch eventually reaches.

[quiz] What would happen if you removed the `if n == 0` base case entirely? | choices: 0) factorial(5) would return 0 1) Python would raise a RecursionError after too many nested calls 2) The function would return 1 immediately 3) The loop would just stop at n = 1 | answer: 1 | why: Without a base case there is no stopping point. Python lets functions nest about 1000 deep, then raises RecursionError to prevent a stack overflow.

[try] Change factorial(5) to factorial(7) and watch the table grow / Change n - 1 to n - 2 and see which base case you need to add / Remove depth=0 and record["depth"] to simplify the code

[next questions] How does Python keep track of all those nested calls? / Where does my phone use recursion without me knowing? / What is the Fibonacci sequence and how do I compute it?

def factorial(n, depth=0):
    record = {"n": n, "depth": depth, "call": f"factorial({n})"}

    if n == 0:               # base case
        record["returns"] = 1
        return 1, [record]

    result, calls = factorial(n - 1, depth + 1)
    answer = n * result
    record["returns"] = answer
    return answer, [record] + calls

content.q: How does binary search find a number so fast?
content.title: Binary search
content.text:
Imagine a phone book with 1,000 pages. You don't start at page 1 — you flip to the middle, decide if your name is in the left or right half, and repeat. **Binary search** does exactly that: it cuts the remaining list in half every single step.

[new word] binary search: An algorithm that finds a value by repeatedly halving the range of places to look. (like Opening a dictionary in the middle, then picking the half your word is in.)

For this to work, the list must be **sorted**. Each time you check the midpoint, you throw away half the candidates — [[9-14|lines 9–14]] pick which half survives. After just 10 cuts you've searched 1,024 items; after 20 cuts, over a million.

Watch the table: notice that `lo`, `mid`, and `hi` chase each other toward index 5 (value 31). The first check [[6|picks the middle]] of all ten items. Because 22 < 31, [[12|lo jumps right]], erasing the whole left side in one move.

The secret sauce is the **sorted order**. Without it you can't know which half to discard — you'd have to check every element. That's why [[11-14|the two branches]] can confidently throw half the work away each round instead of just one item.

How many steps in the worst case? For a list of n items it's about log₂(n) steps. A list of 1,000,000 items takes at most 20 comparisons. Compare that to scanning every item one by one — that's **O(log n)** vs **O(n)**, an enormous difference at scale.

[new word] O(log n): Time complexity where doubling the input adds only one extra step. (like Each fold of a paper halves it — you run out of thickness fast.)

[quiz] The list is [1, 4, 7, 10, 13]. We search for 10. What is the value at mid on the very first check? | choices: 0) 1 1) 7 2) 10 3) 13 | answer: 1 | why: mid = (0 + 4) // 2 = 2, and nums[2] is 7. 7 < 10, so lo moves right for the next step.

[try] Change target to 3 and watch how mid moves left each step / Change target to 99 and see the -1 not-found result / Add 100 to nums without sorting first and notice the wrong answer

[next questions] What happens if there are duplicate numbers in the list? / Where does my phone's contacts search use binary search? / What is a binary search tree and how is it different?
content.code:
def binary_search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    steps = []

    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        steps.append({"lo": lo, "mid": mid, "hi": hi, "value": nums[mid]})

        if nums[mid] == target:
            return steps, mid
        elif nums[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1

    return steps, -1

target = 31
steps, idx = binary_search(nums, target)
show(nums, "sorted list")
show(steps, f"search steps for {target} → index {idx}")

content.q: How does consistent hashing spread keys across servers, and what moves when a server is added?
content.title: Consistent hashing
content.text:
Imagine a ring numbered 0 to 2³²−1. Every server and every key gets **hashed** onto that ring. A key belongs to the first server whose position is ≥ the key's position (wrapping around). With a naive `key % N` scheme, adding one server reshuffles ≈ N−1/N of all keys. Consistent hashing reduces that to ≈ 1/N of keys moving — only the keys between the new node and its predecessor.

[new word] consistent hashing: A scheme where keys are mapped to a fixed ring so only a small fraction move when nodes join or leave. (like Pie slices: adding a new slice only shrinks the one next to it.)

Each server also gets several **virtual nodes** (replicas on the ring). Without them, non-uniform spacing causes one server to absorb a disproportionate share of keys. With *V* virtual nodes per server, the load standard deviation shrinks roughly as 1/√V. The example uses V = 150, a common production default.

[new word] virtual nodes: Extra phantom positions on the ring for one real server, spreading its load more evenly. (like Placing your name in a raffle hat many times.)

The [[5,9|constructor]] hashes each server name V times, producing 150 positions on the ring per server — 450 positions total for three servers. [[19,20|get()]] binary-searches that sorted list in O(log 450) ≈ 9 comparisons. Compare that to a balanced BST over all keys: same asymptotic cost, but here the *ring* is tiny and fixed regardless of key count.

When [[27|_add("s3")]] fires, 150 new positions are inserted. Each new position steals the arc between itself and its predecessor from whatever server previously owned that arc. Keys that hashed into those arcs [[30|move]]; everything else stays put. In a 4-server cluster you expect ≈ 25 % of keys to move — the tables should confirm that number empirically.

**Trade-offs engineers care about:** MD5 is uniform but not cryptographically necessary here; xxHash or MurmurHash3 is faster and equally uniform. V = 150 is a heuristic; Netflix's Dynomite uses 200, Cassandra uses 256. Too-low V produces visible skew in the load bars. Too-high V inflates memory and the O(V·N) insert cost when adding a node. For heterogeneous servers (different capacities), set V proportional to capacity instead of a fixed constant.

[quiz] You have 3 servers and 900 keys perfectly distributed (300 each). You add a 4th server. About how many keys move to the new server? | choices: 0) All 900 — the hash function changes 1) About 225 — only keys in the new server's arc 2) About 600 — every existing server loses half 3) 0 — consistent hashing never moves keys | answer: 1 | why: Each of the 3 existing servers gives up roughly 1/4 of its arc to the new server, so ≈ 300 × (1/4) × 3 = 225 keys move — about 1/N of the total.

content.q: How do promises and async/await work in JavaScript?
content.title: Promises & async/await
content.text:
[new word] promise: An object representing a future value that may succeed or fail. (like A café buzzer — holds your place until the order is ready.)

Before `async/await`, you chained `.then()` calls to react when a promise resolved. `async/await` is just nicer spelling for the same idea: [[14-15|`await` pauses *only this function*]], not the whole program, until the promise settles.

The sequential loop [[14-16|awaits each name one at a time]], so the total time stacks up. Notice the `ms` column in the first table climbs by ~300 each row. The second table using [[21-26|`Promise.all`]] fires all three fetches simultaneously — every `ms` value lands near the same number, roughly 300 ms total.

A **promise** can be in one of three states: *pending* (waiting), *fulfilled* (done, has a value), or *rejected* (failed, has an error). `await` unwraps the value on success; wrap it in `try/catch` to catch rejections, the same way you'd catch a synchronous `throw`.

[new word] Promise.all: Takes an array of promises and returns one promise that resolves when every promise in the array resolves. (like Waiting for the slowest friend — everyone arrives before you leave.)

content.q: What is recursion? Show it with a picture.
content.title: Recursion: a function calls itself
content.text:
Imagine opening a box that contains a smaller box, which contains another—until you reach an empty box. **Recursion** works similarly: a function calls itself with a smaller problem. Our [[1-6|countdown function]] builds a picture of those nested calls.

[new word] recursion: Recursion happens when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of its problem. (like Opening smaller boxes inside a bigger box.)

The picture forms a chain: `countdown(3)` → `countdown(2)` → `countdown(1)` → `countdown(0)`. At [[5|the self-call]], each call subtracts one. These are four separate calls to the same function, each remembering its own `n` and its own box.

The empty box is our **base case**: the situation that needs no smaller call. Here, [[3-4|zero stops the descent]]. Its box returns to the waiting call for one, then two, then three. Each waiting call attaches the returned picture and returns its own box.

[new word] base case: A base case is a situation a function handles without calling itself again. (like The empty box where unpacking stops.)

content.q: How does binary search find a number so fast?
content.title: Find it by halving
content.text:
Imagine finding page 14 in a 16-page booklet: open near the middle, then keep only the side containing your page. **Binary search** does this with numbers in order. Each wrong guess removes about half the remaining possibilities.

[new word] binary search: A way to find a value in an ordered list by repeatedly checking the middle and keeping one half. (like Finding a page by opening halfway through a booklet.)

The table shows guesses **8 → 12 → 14**: just three checks. After 8 is too small, [[10-11|move the left boundary]] past it. After 12 is too small, do that again. The next middle holds 14, so [[8-9|return its position]]: 13, because positions start at zero.

The speed comes from throwing away whole groups, not from guessing luckily. Among 1,024 ordered numbers, even the hardest successful search needs at most 11 checks. This is **logarithmic time**: doubling the list adds at most one extra check. Watch [[5-6|the shrinking search window]] in the table.

[new word] logarithmic time: Work grows slowly: multiplying the input size by a fixed amount adds roughly a fixed number of steps. (like One extra fold lets paper cover twice the thickness.)

The catch: the numbers must already be in increasing order. Otherwise, a smaller middle number tells you nothing reliable about its neighbors. Also, [[7|recording each guess]] helps us watch the search; a practical version can skip that record.

[quiz] Why can the search discard everything through 8 after its first guess? | choices: 0) The list is increasing, so those values cannot be 14. 1) The target always sits in the right half. 2) The first guess must be the smallest number. | answer: 0 | why: Every value through 8 is at most 8. Since 14 is larger, only positions after 8 can contain it.

[try] Change target from 14 to 1. / Change target from 14 to 99. / Change range(1, 17) to range(1, 1025).

[next questions] Why must we skip the middle? / How could a dictionary app use this? / How do we sort an unordered list?
content.code:
def binary_search(numbers, target):
    low = 0
    high = len(numbers) - 1
    steps = []
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        steps.append({"low": low, "middle": mid, "high": high, "guess": numbers[mid]})
        if numbers[mid] == target:
            return mid, steps
        if numbers[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid - 1
    return -1, steps

numbers = list(range(1, 17))
target = 14
index, steps = binary_search(numbers, target)
show(numbers, "Numbers in increasing order")
show(steps, "One row per guess; positions start at zero")
print("Found at position:", index, "Checks:", len(steps))

content.q: How does consistent hashing spread keys across servers, and what moves when a server is added?
content.title: Consistent hashing: who moves?
content.text:
Imagine servers standing around a circular track. Each key gets a position and walks clockwise to the first server. **Consistent hashing** uses this rule so adding a server changes ownership only along one stretch of the track.

[new word] consistent hashing: A way to assign keys to servers that limits reassignment when servers join or leave. (like Adding a collection point along a circular delivery route.)

A **hash function** turns a key into a repeatable number. [[3-4|This function]] places keys at positions 0–99; [[11-14|the lookup]] picks the next server clockwise, wrapping past 99 to A. Different keys can share a position and still remain separate keys.

[new word] hash function: A function that turns an input into a repeatable number. (like A machine that always stamps the same label on the same name.)

Before [[20|adding D at 50]], C owns positions greater than 33 through 66. Afterward, D owns positions greater than 33 through 50; C retains positions greater than 50 through 66. Only keys in that first interval change owners. This code computes destinations; a real storage system must also transfer their stored data.

Spreading keys does not guarantee equal load: larger gaps give servers more keys, and popular keys attract more traffic. Production systems often use **virtual nodes**: several positions per physical server, which smooth ownership at the cost of more bookkeeping. This example uses one position per server and a tiny ring to expose the ownership rule.

[new word] virtual nodes: Multiple positions on the ring assigned to the same physical server. (like One delivery company operating several collection points.)

[quiz] Which keys change owners when D joins at position 50? | choices: 0) Keys at positions greater than 33 through 50 move from C to D. 1) Every key gets a new owner. 2) Keys at positions greater than 50 through 66 move from C to D. | answer: 0 | why: D becomes the first clockwise server only for positions greater than 33 through 50. Those positions previously reached C first.

content.q: How do promises and async/await work in JavaScript?
content.title: Promises and async/await
content.text:
Imagine ordering a sandwich: you get a receipt, then keep chatting while it's made. A **promise** is JavaScript's receipt for a result that will arrive later. In this example, [[6-10|wait]] returns a promise that becomes ready after a timer.

[new word] promise: An object representing a future result that can succeed or fail. (like A receipt for an order still being prepared.)

An **async function** always returns a promise. Calling [[18|run()]] immediately begins its work; its returned promise succeeds when the function finishes. Here, the first two events are recorded before the call returns control to the outside code.

[new word] async function: A function that always returns a promise and allows waiting inside its body. (like A cook who can pause one order while others continue.)

**Await** pauses the surrounding async function until a promise settles. At [[15|await pause]], this promise is still waiting, so outside code records “Outside keeps going.” When the timer completes, the function resumes and records “Sandwich ready.” The measured times may vary; that event order stays the same.

[new word] await: An operation that pauses an async function until a promise succeeds or fails. (like Waiting for your order while the rest of the café carries on.)

The `.then()` method schedules a function to run after a promise succeeds; here it displays the finished table. `await` lets you write that waiting sequence from top to bottom. If an awaited promise fails, it throws an error at the waiting line; use `try/catch` there to handle it.

[quiz] Why does “Outside keeps going” appear before “Sandwich ready”? | choices: 0) Await pauses run, allowing outside code to continue. 1) Async functions wait until all outside code finishes before starting. 2) The timer stops all JavaScript for 30 milliseconds. | answer: 0 | why: Run starts immediately, but pauses at await.
